title: Anchoring Distributed Agency: Institutional Metaphors for Designing Large-Scale AI and AI Techniques for Running Institutions
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) started out with the ambition to reproduce the human mind, but as soon as the sheer scale of that ambition became apparent, it retreated into either studying specialized intelligent behaviours or proposing overarching architectural concepts for interfacing specialized intelligent components---conceived of as agents acting through organizational structures. The agent-based modelling paradigm proved to have interesting applications beyond the original domain, supporting the understanding, simulation, and the assessment of behaviour of socio-economic and legal structures on an aggregate level. Looking at contemporary AI, whereas text completion provides a successful example of specialized behaviour, surprisingly little of the rich foundation of multi-agent systems (MAS) and normative systems research is currently reflected in Agentic AI systems. Addressing this gap, the chapter examines cross-cutting conceptualisations, modelling problems, and design challenges shared by large-scale distributed AI and institutional systems. Three main contributions can be highlighted. First, by tracing the historical trajectory of AI, the chapter identifies an \textit{ecological} perspective on intelligence, examining both the value and limits of the \textit{compression-as-intelligence} hypothesis. Second, it shows how moving between internal cognitive mechanisms and external manifestations of agency supports a functional separation of concerns for both individual and collective agency. Third, it argues that \textit{epistemological}, \textit{normative}, and \textit{value pluralisms} are necessary conditions for sustaining the ecological character of intelligence. Furthermore, we indicate how AI techniques can support institutions by modelling social roles, simulating normative interactions, detecting and diagnosing failures, and supporting procedures of review and revision.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Until recently, analogies between social institutions and computational mind archi- tectures were largely theoretical design metaphors. We spoke of electronic institu- tions as alternatives (or better, complementary) to traditional social arrangements, using institutional vocabulary—norms, roles, and obligations—to conceptualize dis- tributed computational systems. Today, the rise of Agentic AI, driven by large language models (LLMs), has made those theoretical analogies particularly rele- vant. As autonomous (or semi-autonomous) agentic workflows increasingly handle decision-making, task delegation, and execution, the boundary between computa- tional architecture and social organization has blurred. In this context, re-examining the foundational principles of normative multi-agent systems offers a strong ba- sis to identify the challenges for properly governing AI, and more generally socio- technical ecosystems. Drawing from decades-long work in agent-based modeling within the legal do- main, this chapter examines a number of relevant cross-cutting concerns, concep- tualizations, modeling problems, and design challenges that apply equally to large- scale distributed Artificial Intelligence and to the agent-based modeling and simula- tion of social-institutional structures. Our aim is twofold: on the one hand, to provide architectural guidelines for moving beyond a contingent, task-centered, narrow view of AI; on the other hand, to reflect on the deep continuity between institutional and computational domains. However, even if we will explore concerns shared by AI and computer science, and cognitive, social, and legal sciences, we also acknowledge that cross-pollinations between these domains are driven by different motivations. For analytical purposes, this distinction can be formulated as two complex-adaptive- system design problems that draw on overlapping knowledge resources: • the problem of modeling, simulating, and reasoning about complex socio-institutional arrangements like those expressed in law, markets, and accounted for by social stakeholders (institutions, businesses, people) in general; • the problem of designing complex information system arrangements based on design metaphors drawing from vocabulary on minds and institutions. Application domains like electronic institutions were particularly fascinating to re- searchers from both traditions because they required addressing both design prob- lems simultaneously.1 Today, emerging practices of digital governance are increas- ingly articulated through the language of agentic ecosystems, governance harnesses, and programmatic guardrails. These two once-parallel paths have essentially inter- sected: when an enterprise deploys an autonomous AI agent to execute financial contracts, perform medical triage, or manage supply chains, the underlying compu- tational architecture enacts an institutional arrangement, even where that arrange- 1 This is also why the chapter belongs to the present volume. It is not by chance that the notion of anchoring presented in chapter 7 of this volume (Noriega, Padget, and Verhagen, 2026)—that is, the set of pragmatic couplings that must hold for an online institution to be effective within the richer socio-economic-legal environment in which it is situated—matches with the notion of ecological validity we will pursue in our contribution. Anchoring Distributed Agency: Institutional Metaphors and AI Techniques 3 ment remains only partially aligned with the relevant legal, organizational, and so- cial framework. Our present aim therefore is to introduce the main challenges at stake on both sides in a way that inspires the reader to further reflection. For this purpose, we will prefer the construction of a high-level, conceptual framework and scope over an ex- haustive literature review. Our central claim is that robust large-scale AI cannot be understood only as—in terms of today’s core Agentic AI components—model capa- bility plus workflow orchestration. Where a distributed system acts in socially con- sequential settings, its architecture also allocates epistemic access, practical powers, duties, evidential burdens, and opportunities to contest decisions and revise proce- dures. These are institutional functions. Conversely, institutions increasingly need computational methods to represent social roles, diagnose failures, and test or re- vise procedures under varying conditions of complexity and pluralism. The paper proceeds as follows. Section 2 will provide a historical reflection on the trajectory of the AI discipline, starting from understanding and modelling the “mind”, suffering from the scaling problem, and focusing on engineering in- telligence piece by piece. Section 3 will cover relevant perspectives on individual agency, while section 4 will focus on institutions and collective agency. Section 5 examines several forms of pluralism and connects them to ecological diversity. In the concluding discussion section (Section 6), we identify a number of poten- tial grounds for novel advances in the application of institutional metaphors to dis- tributed AI, and the application of AI techniques in modeling, analyzing, and eval- uating socio-institutional arrangements. 2 From modelling to engineering, from individuals to ecologies 2.1 Modeling the Mind As a discipline, Artificial Intelligence (AI) started out with the ambition to repro- duce the human mind as a monolithic computer program. The problem of reproduc- ing intelligence in technology was approached primarily as a functional decomposi- tion exercise, with “intelligence” serving as the high-level function to be recreated within a software system by combining smaller functions realized through simple, well-understood input-output modules. It was only later that machine learning ap- proaches rose to dominance, eventually becoming nearly synonymous with AI to- day; these focus primarily on the functional reproduction of intelligent behavior, rather than its structured, controlled decomposition. The nature of constituent primitive modules was rather clear to early com- puter scientists: logical inference and knowledge structures were expected to play a key role, informed by introspection, common-sense psychology, and contemporary concepts of rationality (Newell and Simon, 1976). The General Problem Solver (Newell, Shaw, and Simon, 1959) may be considered the archetype of this approach 4 Alexander Boer and Giovanni Sileno and is frequently cited as such in lectures on the history of AI. In architectures of this type, scaling up from simple toy examples of reasoning to plausible intelligent function, even within restricted cognitive niches, becomes a challenge of manag- ing complex knowledge in a logic-based representation language, where the formal properties of the logic enforce modularity and prevent unwanted interactions be- tween represented knowledge structures. As soon as this required modularity breaks down—that is, when knowledge structures interact in unforeseen and undesirable ways—the construction of the higher-level function (intelligence) may catastrophically fail. If we are lucky, it fails obviously, such as when constraints enforced by the representation language are violated; more insidiously, it fails through unintelligent behavior in many other cases. From an engineering perspective, an AI system following this architectural paradigm lacks sufficient adaptive capacity, or resilience, to reliably incorporate new knowledge structures. 2.2 The Scaling Problem, and Beyond It The scaling problem in an architecture based on logical inference and knowledge structures, continually presents itself as a knowledge representation bottleneck: background knowledge is always too sparse to properly scope knowledge struc- tures, causing the system to eventually draw inferences that are untrue and, more critically, obviously unintelligent. Historically, this limitation led to several distinct tracks of AI research: • to uncover and formalize implicit background assumptions—such as the infa- mous frame problem (Morgenstern, 1996)—that are typically overlooked and threaten system modularity; • to codify massive volumes of common-sense background knowledge for general AI use (Lenat, 1995), in the hope of eventually achieving critical mass; • to identify foundational knowledge structures with universal applicability— codifying them into formal top-level ontologies (Sowa, 1995) for reuse across distributed modules; and • to scope defeasibility in logical reasoning (Pollock, 1975) by designing non- monotonic logics and representation languages that contain undesirable inter- actions between knowledge structures. Research that addresses these problems belongs historically to the symbolic AI tradition. Perhaps its main impact was to steer the mainstream philosophy of the field away from the initial strict mathematical logic—and a disdain for logical in- consistency and irrationality—toward more psychologically valid views of reason- ing and human rationality. A further, partly complementary response to the scaling problem was to decom- pose the AI problem into two more manageable challenges, allowing AI researchers to focus on either: Anchoring Distributed Agency: Institutional Metaphors and AI Techniques 5 1. studying well-defined, specialized intelligent behaviors (e.g., playing chess, rec- ognizing human faces, or solving job-shop scheduling problems) within specific contexts of use; or 2. proposing overarching architectural concepts for interfacing specialized intelli- gent components. These are conceived of as agents—each competent in a limited set of behaviors—operating within a virtual organization to project the appear- ance of a single, generally intelligent agent to the outside world. We examine the impact of these two research trajectories in more detail. 2.2.1 On specialized intelligent behaviours Solving the first type of problem yields direct, viable commercial applications that justify research funding, though in the past it was often dismissed as “not real AI” due to its lack of adaptive potential. Yet, ironically, contemporary public usage of the term AI overwhelmingly refers to applications of this kind. Chatbots based on Large Language Models (LLMs), for example, are typically centred on a large neu- ral model trained to predict and generate text, embedded within architectural lay- ers that sustain dialogue, manage interaction, and shape outputs through instruction tuning and alignment methods such as reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) (Ouyang et al., 2022). Nothing in these specialized systems explicitly ad- dresses general intelligence. What appears to be general intelligence is, in fact, a side-effect of language being a general-purpose human interface. Yet, the possibil- ity of codifying massive background knowledge brought the consequence that the search for universally appealing knowledge structures has migrated from top on- tologies or explicit common-sense knowledge representations (a core research track in symbolic AI) to learned latent representations (although at the price of opacity, hallucinations, and possibly ill-formed structures). 2.2.2 On organizational architectures Addressing the second challenge—proposing overarching architectures for agent coordination—historically received far less attention than the first one beyond AI research. These architectural questions gained public visibility through debates on the responsibility gap created by the widespread deployment of autonomous and distributed systems, such as algorithmic trading agents, autonomous vehicles, and weapons systems like drone swarms (Matthias, 2004). They have now re-emerged as a practical, though still largely under-theorised, concern in the development of modern Agentic AI systems. Broadly defined, “Agentic AI” refers to AI systems engineered to operate au- tonomously or semi-autonomously (with minimal user intervention). Moving be- yond passive, turn-based text generation, these systems proactively plan, reason, and direct multi-step workflows while adapting to dynamic environments to achieve higher-level goals. As this field evolves, new terminology is rapidly emerging— 6 Alexander Boer and Giovanni Sileno often shaped through bottom-up engineering practices rather than structured theo- retical reflection. Central to this landscape is the concept of agent harness (or scaf- folding): the software architecture that encapsulates core foundation models—most importantly large language models (LLMs) or multimodal models with LLM her- itage. In essence, a harness acts as the execution engine, managing state and mem- ory, driving the decision-making control loop, executing tool calls, handling error recovery, and enforcing security boundaries. From this point of view, modern agentic architectures synthesize both histori- cal strains of AI research: the underlying foundation models handle functional re- production, whereas the agent harness provides an operational functional decom- position framework. Reframing these developments through debates on multi-agent coordination and normative systems can therefore provide stronger conceptual foun- dations for their design and governance. 2.3 Engineering a Mind as an Ecology of Minds For the purposes of this chapter, we are mainly concerned with the second challenge: overarching architectural concepts. Archetypal for this response are the agents in the visionary Society of Mind of Minsky (1986) (“The power of intelligence stems from our vast diversity, not from any single, perfect principle”, p. 308), as well as the concrete intelligent creatures proposed by Brooks (1991) in his seminal work “Intelligence without representation”. According to Brooks, the fundamental de- composition of intelligence should not rely on modules that interface via a shared, centralized knowledge representation; rather, it should consist of independent crea- tures that interact directly with their environment through perception and action, ex- hibiting ecological validity within that domain. The central insight here is to bring to the foreground the tight coupling between an agent—or creature—and its host environment, niche, or ecology. Specialized intelligent behaviors within a specific niche can often be successfully isolated. Some problems, such as playing chess, may be tackled using specialized, explicit knowledge representations paired with appropriate search algorithms. Oth- ers, such as face recognition, are less amenable to solution through introspection; in AI systems, they are achieved not through knowledge representation techniques, but via machine learning algorithms operating on vast datasets of labeled examples that exemplify the behavior to be acquired. Large Language Models (LLMs)—operating fundamentally as systems optimized for text completion—fall directly into this cate- gory. However, there is a key difference: cracking a problem like chess as a symbolic search problem means becoming able to generate at need ecologically valid labeled examples—essentially trusted synthetic data. This data can be subsequently used for machine learning, resulting in efficient, scalable machine learning chess with comparable performance. The reverse direction remains very difficult: recovering an explicit and accountable symbolic representation from an opaque learned model denotes an unresolved explainability problem, addressed in the neuro-symbolic re- Anchoring Distributed Agency: Institutional Metaphors and AI Techniques 7 search stream. The third route—using the outputs of one learned model as unexam- ined training data for another, is problematic. Recursive reliance on synthetic data may produce unintentional and unrecognised distributional distortions or model col- lapse (Shumailov et al., 2024); where the generated data is maliciously manipulated or insufficiently controlled, it may also create data-poisoning risks. This strength- ens the case for accountable generative mechanisms of behaviour where they can be constructed. 2.3.1 Multi-Agent Systems, and IBM’s Watson, and beyond Historically, the challenge of finding architectural concepts to create and maintain the appearance of a single, unified agent led to the development of multi-agent sys- tems (MAS). These architectures consist of multiple autonomous agents interacting within a shared environment, each operating with its own perception–action loop and without global knowledge of the system as a whole (e.g. Ferber and Weiss, 1999). A central concern in decentralised MAS research is to avoid reliance on a single controller or globally shared memory, because such arrangements may recreate the brittleness associated with centralised functional decomposition. Re- searchers investigated decentralized organizational models and peer-level coordina- tion mechanisms, aimed at enhancing overall system resilience and adaptive capac- ity (e.g. Wooldridge, 2009). Yet, although multi-agent system research has yielded many valuable theoretical insights into organizational dynamics (e.g. Dignum, 2009; Grossi et al., 2006), few examples of practical value successfully combined relevant sets of intelligent behaviors within this traditional paradigm. It is instructive, how- ever, to examine the first well-known system that demonstrated significant success in matching specialized computational creatures to specific problem niches: IBM’s Watson (Ferrucci et al., 2010). Watson gained widespread fame for its decisive victory on the game show Jeop- ardy!. From our architectural perspective, Watson performed essentially one core task: question answering (QA). Yet, its internal architecture operated as a coali- tion of distinct QA agents that compete against one another to generate the highest- scoring response. In its essence, the system relied on giving conditionally atten- tion to different representation subspaces embodied by the different ‘creatures’.2 Through the competitive dynamic, the system evaluated the candidate responses and learned to select the optimal answer based on features extracted from both the query and the candidate solutions. This competitive architecture represented a compelling departure from brittle functional decomposition, pointing instead toward more ro- bust organizational metaphors. Related principles of specialisation, conditional se- lection, or comparative evaluation appear across machine-learning paradigms, in- cluding generative adversarial networks (GANs) (Goodfellow et al., 2014), ensem- ble techniques like random decision forests (Tin Kam Ho, 1995), mixture of experts 2 Strictly speaking, Watson was not a decentralised multi-agent system in the strong sense. Yet, it still illustrates how specialised computational perspectives can be comparatively evaluated rather than collapsed into a single inference chain. 8 Alexander Boer and Giovanni Sileno (MoEs) (Jacobs et al., 1991; Shazeer et al., 2017), actor-critic reinforcement learn- ing (Konda and Tsitsiklis, 1999). However, the structural and social scaffolding gov- erning these statistical models remain comparatively minimal. In some respects, Watson’s ensemble of specialised question-answering com- ponents anticipates patterns now found in LLM-based agent orchestration. While Watson relied on hand-crafted feature extractors and a statistically weighted arbiter within a closed domain, contemporary Agentic AI frameworks rely on dynamic, contingently instantiated (and dissolved) “societies” or ensembles of LLM-powered components, in which distinct personas or specialized sub-agents debate, critique, and refine intermediate outputs through an overarching agent harness. These com- ponents are often described as agents, even when their autonomy remains limited and the overall workflow is centrally orchestrated. Multi-head attention allows a LLM to attend jointly to different representational aspects of its input; multi-agent orchestration of LLM-powered agents can instead distribute work across differenti- ated prompts, tools, models, or perspectives. In short, by coupling decentralized multi-agent coordination with state/memory management and external tool access, contemporary Agentic AI implicitly attempts to realize the organizational metaphors envisioned by multi-agent systems research, transforming static statistical text generation into adaptive, goal-directed problem solving. It is therefore crucial to bring this vision to the foreground—both to re- examine the identified challenges and to chart a principled way forward. 2.3.2 Agent-Based Modelling, and beyond Multi-agent system technologies and concepts have thus far achieved their greatest success indirectly, serving as the foundation for the agent-based modeling (ABM) paradigm, with notable applications in understanding, simulating, and, in controlled settings, anticipating the macro-behavior of real-world socio-legal structures (Conte and Paolucci, 2014; Railsback and Grimm, 2019). However, agent-based modeling addresses a fundamentally different class of problems—in many ways dual to the ecological perspective outlined above—concerning the internal primitives required to specify an individual agent’s behavior. Whereas specifications based on simple reflex architectures or quantitative utility functions may suffice for studying aggre- gate systemic phenomena under stylised assumptions of economic rationality, hu- man discourse concerning social actors typically invokes intentional and normative categories, prioritizing qualitative dimensions of behavior. To bridge this gap, research since the early 1990s has advanced the study of cognitive agents (e.g. Rao and Georgeff, 1992) and normative multi-agent sys- tems (NMAS) (e.g. Boella, Torre, and Verhagen, 2006), aiming to establish com- putational infrastructures grounded in inferential interpretive templates drawn from practical reasoning, folk psychology, law, institutional economics, and linguistics. The theory of mind tradition is exemplified by the belief-desire-intention (BDI) agent architecture (Bratman, 1987), while formal frameworks for normative posi- tions draw extensively on classical literature concerning norms (Alchourr´on and Anchoring Distributed Agency: Institutional Metaphors and AI Techniques 9 Bulygin, 1971), jural relations (Hohfeld, 1913), and speech acts (Austin, 1975). Crucially, the purpose of these formalisms is not necessarily to provide empirically faithful models of human cognitive processing. Their purpose is to provide high- level and precise specifications of agent behaviour in terms that remain intelligible to human participants, and that can guide or govern autonomous execution within complex socio-technical arrangements. They aim, in other words, to make the rele- vant structures of agency explicit, inspectable, and open to revision. 3 Agency as Unity 3.1 External and Internal Views In abstract terms, all problems reviewed in the previous section are expressions of a fundamental tension between unity and multiplicity. Multiplicity arises where unity fails, or to achieve what cannot be accomplished by individuals alone. Multiplic- ity is composed of unities which, when viewed in aggregate, may constitute a new unity; conversely, unities may recursively contain internal multiplicities. This on- tological duality gives rise to two co-existing perspectives: the external view (ad- dressing a system-unity acting within an environment) and the internal view (ad- dressing a system composed of multiple interacting components). For example, an organization can be viewed externally as a single socio-economic actor that con- sumes and produces resources (e.g., products, services) to achieve specific goals; internally, it appears as an arrangement of roles embodied by individual employ- ees, supported by a network of business units, subsidiary organizations, and coor- dinated partners. Similarly, a decision-support system or the guidance system of an autonomous vehicle may be perceived externally as a unified software artifact pro- ducing task-relevant outputs from given computational and informational resources, while internally functioning as a complex of interconnected modules providing the necessary execution functions. Unsurprisingly, this distinction between internal and external views is embedded in standard modeling practices (e.g., UML) and soft- ware engineering paradigms, reflected in concepts such as orchestration and chore- ography. Yet this raises a fundamental question: Why is an entity perceived as a unity externally and as a multiplicity internally? More precisely, as we are dealing with entities designed to act within the world, what does it mean for a multi-component system to successfully project the appearance of a single agent to the outside world? The question is not merely conceptual. In terms of legal accountability, for instance, obligations are ascribed to providers and deployers of an AI system as legally singu- lar entities, whatever the internal multiplicity of the artefact. In terms of operations, an agent harness may hide multi-component workflows behind a single interface; the system is thereby presented as one coherent agent, even where its internal oper- ation is distributed. 10 Alexander Boer and Giovanni Sileno The remainder of this section develops this distinction in two directions: first, by examining the interpretive conditions under which a complex arrangement is treated as a unified agent; second, by identifying the agentive positions required to specify, explain, and govern its conduct. 3.2 What Agents Look Like, Externally When interpreting a scene, observers frame events depending on the most pertinent analytical perspective available to them. In a classic illustration by Hart and Honor´e (1985), a farmer may view a drought as the primary cause of a severe famine, whereas an international body might attribute responsibility to the host government for failing to establish adequate food reserves. Plausible criteria identified within cognitive science as governing an observer’s choice of analytical stance include informativity—the capacity to draw actionable conclusions tied to the observer’s values or interests—and the required cognitive effort (cf. relevance theory (Sperber and Wilson, 1986) and simplicity theory (Dessalles, 2013)). Among the interpretive attitudes available to an observer, Dennett’s intentional stance (Dennett, 1987) is inherently more vulnerable to prediction errors than phys- ical or design-based stances, yet it yields highly informative explanations at a frac- tion of the cognitive cost. For instance, explaining a child’s movement toward a bowl of sweets by analyzing their underlying physiological state or evolutionary history would ordinarily be far less tractable, and far less informative for practical purposes, than attributing a desire for the sweets and a belief that they are avail- able. The same economy of explanation often governs the external interpretation of complex collectives—such as organisations and nation-states—as well as the inter- pretation of AI systems as unified intentional agents. 3.3 Intentional Ascriptions and Articulations as Reasons In adopting an intentional stance, observers attribute beliefs, desires, and intentions to an agent, treating it as a rational entity—namely, one that “will act to further its goals in the light of its beliefs” (Dennett, 1987)—to construct a reasonable approx- imation of its trajectory. Viewing intentional ascription as the attribution of reasons for conduct connects it to the broader phenomenon of mentalisation (Fonagy and Target, 1997): interpreting behaviour in terms of beliefs, desires, intentions, and other purposive states. In formal settings, the same move supports a rationalisa- tion of behaviour, namely the reconstruction of the reasons by which conduct can be explained or justified. Ultimately, an entity—whether a person, an institution, or an artificial system—is interpreted as an agent because observers can successfully ascribe beliefs, desires, and intentions to it in order to yield reliable predictions. Anchoring Distributed Agency: Institutional Metaphors and AI Techniques 11 The same dynamic holds introspectively when an agent observes its own behavior, articulating its internal motivations as explicit reasons for action. Both having articulated beliefs, desires, and intentions, and being able to ascribe beliefs, desires, and intentions to another agent clearly facilitate communication among social entities. Mercier and Sperber (2011) make this point forcefully: evo- lutionarily speaking, the primary function of reasoning using explicit knowledge structures must be argumentation. This insight is supported both by the historical emergence of human socio-institutional systems and by the increasingly central role that multi-agent deliberation plays in contemporary Agentic AI. However, a different outcome might be expected depending on whether we adopt the agent or the observer point of view. Traditional experiments on confirmation bias in human reasoning consistently reveal a striking asymmetry between produc- ing and evaluating arguments: when generating arguments for a claim, individuals exhibit a strong confirmation bias, selectively gathering and remembering support- ing evidence; conversely, when evaluating or arguing against a claim, they become remarkably adept at detecting and refuting weak, biased arguments. Mercier and Sperber (2011) connect these psychological findings to the rationality of dialectical argumentation—such as in a legal trial—where a process governed by adversarial competition systematically promotes discovering truth, even when individual par- ticipants are merely striving to win. A central mechanism of any court (or dialectal) setting is the burden of proof— the procedural obligation to supply evidence for asserted claims (Walton, 1988). Burdens of proof are systematically allocated to agents based on whether establish- ing a claim advances an actor’s dialectical position. Within legal norm structures, these obligations can generally be allocated statically to the propositional condi- tions of a rule. When viewed through the lens of the burden of proof, the charge of individual cognitive irrationality in argument production loses its force: generating biased, self-interested arguments is not a flaw, but a functional strategy within an adversarial protocol.3 The central question of “rationalization” shifts therefore to the design of the com- munication setting, the allocation of burdens, and the identification of those charged with arguing against a claim (Gordon, Prakash, and Prakken, 2007). Institutionally, this concerns how normative rules can be structurally attached to particular commu- nication settings, and which elements of a rule serve which institutional interests. To preserve a separation between argument production and evaluation, evaluators should not have access to precisely the same reasons available to producers, and vice versa. In an Agentic AI system implementing a generate & verify orchestration, as long as the verifier is looking at the same buffer and employs the same LLM (so it shares parametric knowledge) of the generator, it will take all input as its own and be de- fensive about it. For an argumentative setting to function, the verifier must maintain some form of information asymmetry—having access to only a limited portion of 3 In this light, behaviours routinely diagnosed as problematic in LLMs, such as post-hoc rationali- sation or the production of plausible but weakly grounded reasons, appear not to be isolated defects of generation, but resulting from the alignment with the role of a producer of arguments. 12 Alexander Boer and Giovanni Sileno the generator’s knowledge.4 In other words, effectively challenging arguments re- quires some degree of independence. 3.4 Scripting Behaviour and the Resulting Ecology But how can an observer ascribe a determinate course of action to an agent when the space of behaviour open to that agent is, for practical purposes, vast and underde- termined? In traditional decision theory, a rational decision-maker selects a solution by maximizing expected utility over candidate options. This optimization principle underlies the homo oeconomicus view in classical economics: actors are assumed to be self-interested entities that systematically maximize their utility functions. There are many ways in which one can frame criticisms against these assump- tions and account instead for the boundedness of human rationality, starting from the obvious observation that decision problems in the real world are often too complex, making it practically impossible to perform maximization over all potential alter- natives. Heuristics, rules, and procedures emerge as an agent’s effective responses to unpredictable errors in selecting optimal solutions. Heiner (1983) identifies the root of this general phenomenon in the gap between an agent’s competence at solv- ing a problem and the difficulty of that problem within a given environment—the competence-difficulty (C-D) gap. Heiner convincingly argues that under large C-D gaps, an agent generally per- forms more effectively and efficiently over time by following simple rules rather than attempting full optimization. For instance, a skilled chess player tends to play routine openings to capitalize on past experience with the board states that develop from those lines, exercising greater creativity only in the middle and late game— even though standard interpretations of rationality might suggest that calculating optimal moves becomes easier as board complexity decreases late in the game. In social settings, this dynamic leads to the institutionalization of interactions, as par- ticipants perform better when behavior remains mutual and predictable. Similarly, while there are numerous valid ways to conclude a commercial transaction, a su- permarket accommodates only a single routine to structure the interaction and min- imize cognitive load. The result is that the agent engages in a form of ecological niche construction (Bardone, 2011), associating relatively simple rule sets with the social roles it enacts when interacting with an environment, depending on its model of that environment. 4 See for instance (Xu, Li, and Jiang, 2025), showing that candidates who use the same LLM to write or tailor their resume as the one used by the recruiter/evaluator experience a 23% to 60% increase in shortlist likelihood, regardless of underlying differences in human qualification. Anchoring Distributed Agency: Institutional Metaphors and AI Techniques 13 3.5 Social Intelligence as Compressing Behaviour In simplified terms, an agent and its environment can be modeled as interacting pro- grams that exchange discrete symbols, where the environment emits reward signals in response to the agent’s actions. Along related lines, Legg and Hutter (2007) de- fine intelligent behavior as an agent’s expected reward within a given environment, extending this to universal intelligence when evaluated across all computable envi- ronments. The agent’s core task is to predict which output sequences will maximize cumulative future reward—a formulation that encompasses domains such as strate- gic game-playing (where competence relies on inferring an opponent’s strategy), as well as question-answering (predicting responses that optimize evaluative feed- back), text completion, and, at higher level of complexity, maintaining its functions in an open environment. To predict competently, the agent must effectively infer the underlying generative program executing within its environment. This challenge is formally equivalent to data compression: discovering a minimal program (the predictive model) capable of reproducing the observed environmental dynamics. This equivalence motivated the creation of the Hutter Prize (Hutter, 2006), which rewards advances in compressing large text corpora under the premise that compression efficiency is intrinsically tied to general intelligence. A similar intuition is formalized within algorithmic infor- mation theory, captured by Chaitin’s dictum that “understanding is compression” (Chaitin, 2005). Today, the “intelligence as compression” has transitioned from the- oretical algorithmic information theory to a central tenet of modern technology: LLMs are, at their core, massive lossy compression engines that compress internet- scale human text into neural network parameters to predict subsequent tokens. Yet, despite being a powerful abstraction, intelligence as compression has clear limita- tions from an ecological point of view (Dowe, Hern´andez-Orallo, and Das, 2011).5 First, compression alone does not determine what should count as relevant sig- nal, valuable performance, or acceptable error, i.e. reward mechanisms. In lossy compression schemes (such as audio and video compression), we discard parts of environmental data as noise rather than signal because they are irrelevant to the human observer—that is, no reward penalty is incurred. Contemporary LLM- centered systems explicitly address this by incorporating internal or external align- ment mechanisms (such as RLHF, direct preference optimizations, or “constitu- tional” guardrails) to supply this evaluative signal. Yet, without an inherent external frame of reference, we have no theoretical account of how an autonomous agent distinguishes between useful signal and irrelevant noise; attempting to compress ev- erything universally is ecologically invalid as a response to the cognitive limitations of an agent operating within a complex environment. In short, a comprehensive the- ory of intelligence must directly address Heiner’s C-D gap. The second limitation deals with social environments, and is in this context ob- vious. It cannot account for shared vocabulary between agents (i.e., an ontology), nor with argumentation, and not with the exchange of instructions and normative rules be- tween agents. Any account of these omissions would need to explain how agents, de- spite their diverse experiences, keep their programs sufficiently similar to exchange pieces of them with other agents. In contemporary AI, this problem cannot be resolved by internal model align- ment alone, as it intrinsically concerns the external, inter-subjective manifestations of agency. Nor is it covered by “constitutional AI” approaches, as these techniques are conceived for an individual model to critique and refine its own outputs, rather than to orchestrate a heterogeneous collective of social actors. Current attempts to supplement frozen foundation models with memory, interaction, or multi-agent feedback remain limited in their capacity for reciprocal and institutionally structured adaptation. Designing an institutional architecture—including open communication protocols, contractual mechanisms, and normative governance frameworks—is one of the core concerns of normative multi-agent systems (NMAS). Nevertheless, the core insight of the intelligence-as-compression paradigm re- mains of interest even with NMAS: when confronted with a complex environment or a peer agent, intelligence entails the capacity to construct or select a generative program that accurately models that entity, alongside a correlative program (or pol- icy) designed to drive fulfilling and rewarding interactions with it. 3.6 Specifying Intentional Agents The traditional AI perspective internalizes the intentional stance and considers agents as intelligent systems—entities performing certain actions to achieve specific goals, conditioned upon their knowledge. Consider, for instance, the uncompromis- ingly external perspective towards agents taken by Newell in his seminal paper on the knowledge level (Newell, 1982). Knowledge and goals are ascribed to an agent to explain its behavior, remaining separable from the structures and mechanisms that create that behavior. In a sense, Newell proposes to create models of observed agent behavior within the bounds of some design constraints, operating via a model of deliberation loosely referred to as the principle of rationality. The question of how to reproduce the mechanisms that create the behavior is secondary, and in prac- tice often easier if the design problem is well-defined and the goals of the agent are easy to identify (such as in constrained domains like chess or facial recognition). In more open-ended settings, where goals are dynamic and need to be contin- uously re-set, this simplification no longer holds. Connecting goals to the broader category of desires, we can approach the traditional philosophical account of practi- cal rationality based on a belief-desire (BD) architecture. Bratman (1987) convinc- ingly argued against such two-parameter characterizations, highlighting the crucial role of intentions (I). In a BDI framework, agents may hold conflicting, inconsis- tent desires—such as desiring both to eat chocolate and to adhere to a weight-loss Anchoring Distributed Agency: Institutional Metaphors and AI Techniques 15 plan—yet the subset of desires eventually selected to govern actual conduct must be mutually consistent against the backdrop of beliefs. It is this active selection, reified as intention, that captures the distinctively deliberative aspect of agency. However, for the reasons outlined above, in contrast to the traditional view of a deliberative agent—according to which agents make rational decisions by weighing competing reasons—one could instead start from an interpretative basis, consider- ing that agents reproduce established courses of action (or scripts).6 Scripts sedi- ment deliberations that have occurred previously: they associate recurrent situations with socially or operationally established responses. Intentions, as commitments to specific courses of action, are then reduced once more to lower-order (concrete, contingent) volitional states selected by higher-order (generic, structural) desires in accordance with the abilities and knowledge ascribed to the agent, alongside the perceived state of the environment. Evidently, insights gained from an interpretative standpoint can be remapped in generative terms: viewed from within the agent’s internal architecture, these same mental states serve as the drivers of its conduct. An agent behaves in a specific man- ner precisely to satisfy its intents. Whether such mental states possess literal onto- logical status or are merely epiphenomena of underlying neural or computational processes is irrelevant with respect to their functional utility. Indeed, the founda- tional principle of responsibility in socio-legal systems relies on the pragmatic as- sumption that such intentional states are indispensable for reasoning about human behavior. 3.7 Agentive Positions Upon closer inspection, the standard belief-desire-intention (BDI) triad can be fur- ther expanded. The classical BDI template lacks for instance explicit primitives for representing agentic abilities (which condition the action-selection process) and sensory capabilities (which determine which elements of the environment are per- ceptible to the agent).7 To bridge this gap, in previous work (Sileno, 2016; Sileno, Boer, and van Engers, 2015) we recognized four primitive categories required to specify the behavior of an agent: commitments, affordances, expectations, and sus- ceptibilities (CAES). Informally, these correspond to what the agent wants, what (it perceives) it is able to do, what it believes, and what it is disposed to react to. Any instance of these classes constitutes a position assumed by the agent with respect to its environment. These include commitments that are acceptable to the agent (desires), those that are preferred, and finally those that are selected as objectives or intents, which sub- sequently trigger an intention associated with a specific course of action (or plan). Technically, introducing prioritization at the preference level resolves potential in- ternal inconsistencies, enabling a conflict-free selection of desires to be committed to as intents. From a generative perspective, commitments can be interpreted as agentic dispositions possessing sufficient stability to drive sustained conduct. More- over, reasons for action do not always reduce to concrete objectives; desires promot- ing abstract values profoundly influence agent behavior, albeit operating at a deeper level of rationalization. Expectations (E) reflect the situatedness of the subject in the world, capturing what the agent believes the world is, both actually and poten- tially. The actual category mirrors traditional beliefs, whereas the potential category designates what the agent projects the world may bring about under specific con- ditions, incorporating causal dynamics. Within the intelligence-as-compression hy- pothesis, expectations fulfill the role of the generative program executed by the envi- ronment, which the agent leverages to maximize rewards relative to its active com- mitments. Affordances (or abilities, A) represent action opportunities—the possibil- ities for an agent to enact specific behaviors under given environmental conditions to achieve designated outcomes. Affordances interact dynamically with commitments to determine which behavioral trajectory is ultimately selected. Susceptibilities (or sensory capabilities, S) capture the reactive dimension of agency; an agent exhibits susceptibility to a given event if it registers a reaction to its occurrence at either the epistemic or motivational level. The CAES template supports both explanatory and generative inferences. At its core lies the possibility of a conflict between an active commitment and an ex- pectation concerning the current state of the world. From an explanatory perspec- tive, such a conflict can support abductive intent ascription: it helps explain why an agent acted. From a generative perspective, it can initiate action selection: the agent searches for an available course of action capable of reducing or resolving the conflict. Beyond this foundational control loop, the CAES template enables us to capture additional functional dependencies, including: • enactive perception (mapping from active commitments C to a susceptibility S): perceptual experience must be coupled with the agent’s active course of action, primarily to anticipate potential (often negative) outcomes through continuous monitoring; • affordance activation (mapping from active expectations E to an affordance A): because epistemic conflicts are evaluated at a higher level, an auxiliary infor- mational channel is required to contextualize the agent’s capabilities within the current situation; • affordance inhibition (mapping from a stronger commitment C′ to A): when a contemplated action generates consequences that conflict with higher-priority desires, the associated affordance is inhibited to prevent execution, even if per- ceived. Anchoring Distributed Agency: Institutional Metaphors and AI Techniques 17 These dependencies can be related, at a high level of abstraction, to techniques found in contemporary Agentic AI. Enactive perception has loose analogues in relevance filtering, retrieval selection, and context-window management; affordance activation resembles context-sensitive tool availability, such as dynamic API-schema injection or state-dependent function calling; and affordance inhibition resembles program- matic safety boundaries, including permission checks, execution interceptors, and guardrail mechanisms. The CAES framework is not reducible to these engineering techniques, however, because it specifies the functional roles that such mechanisms may play within a broader architecture of agency. Consider, for instance, an assistant managing a task board. Initially, the agent possesses a basic affordance (A): posting tasks. When a user requests coding assis- tance, perceiving this input (S) leads the agent to commit to this request (C) and then to apply the associated affordance (A). Taking this commitment also produces explicit expectations (E) regarding task completion shared with the user, while dy- namically activating new context-dependent affordances (A)—such as file system manipulation and local code execution. These tools remain available until an ex- plicit discharge by the user (S) clears the task from the board, updating the agent’s active commitments (C) and restoring baseline susceptibilities (S). 4 Institutions and Collective Agency 4.1 Going Internal: Control vs. Ecological Structures The external point of view serves as the basis for interpretation, whereas the internal viewpoint is foundational for design. In social and computational systems alike, the implementation layer consists of interacting actors, components, and artifacts, some of which may possess varying degrees of autonomy (agents). System design there- fore concerns establishing structural arrangements that enable and support those elements in forming and maintaining robust organizations to achieve higher-order goals. Such arrangements typically combine cooperation, coordination, and compe- tition, under conditions of bounded information exchange and only partial commit- ment to shared vocabularies and behavioural rules. Evidently, distributing operational and computational loads across relatively in- dependent agents can shift system design away from tightly integrated control struc- tures and toward more decentralised ecological structures. If there is only one module that implements a required function for the IT service to function and this module fails, the application will stop working properly. A distinguishing factor of coordination schemes is the presence of explicit signal- ing. For instance, symbiosis persists even without explicit communication, whereas institutions cannot exist without some form of language (not necessarily verbal). 4.2 The Central Role of Failures Institutions are indeed prototypical examples of mechanisms of coordination: they build upon symbolic means and form an infrastructure providing incentives (in the form of rewards and punishments, or the proverbial “carrots” and “sticks”) to social actors, thereby modifying the incentives available from the non-institutional envi- ronment. Competitive dynamics are instead generally extra-institutional (e.g., the choice of a sale price in a market). The primary practical function of a legal system is not only to set expectations among social participants, but also to intervene when an institutional failure is pre- sumed to occur in social interactions—i.e., when the institutional expectations of one of the parties involved are not met. Ex-post judicial interpretations are meant to make explicit the normative positions of the parties prior to the failure, and then to associate an institutional response if the failure is confirmed, building upon the sources of law. Within this perspective, legal sources operate as reasons for enrich- ing and revising the behavioural models ascribed to the parties. The centrality of failure is perhaps the strongest point of contrast between the in- stitutional and the common engineering treatment of norms. Engineering practice— and machine-learning practice even more so—is organized around aggregate per- formance on the expected case.8 A legal system is organized around the exceptional case, and specifically around the case in which someone complains. This is not a deficiency of either system; it reflects the fact that institutions exist to handle what could not be anticipated at design time, which is why the ex-post interpretive mo- ment cannot be compiled away. In effect, one can recognize here a basis for the famous trias politica. The executive, legislative, and judiciary branches can be seen as con- centrating, respectively, the directive and executive, the regulative and publishing, and the interpretative and declarative functions of a collective agency. The principle of the separation of powers can be explained as aiming to maintain the balances present in the standard reasoning architecture. If the same actor holds, e.g., both the directive and interpretative powers, there is a short-circuit in the architecture be- cause interpretation could be forced to enable this actor’s commitments, rather than respecting those consolidated in the norms. Many interventions of the judiciary occur today on an asynchronous basis: the triggering event consists of a social actor (the plaintiff) that supposedly experienced an institutional failure and goes to the court. This means that monitoring power is left to individual social participants. However, the wide presence of global online platforms, as well as of institutional administrative digital repositories, has opened possibilities for upstream monitoring of several types of socio-economic transac- tions by entities having access to such information. De Mulder and Meijer (2012) have argued for an extension of the principle of the separation of powers to a tetras politica, incorporating these potential monitoring branches. According to our archi- tectural analysis, their argument is sound. In a distributed system, monitoring effort is supported by attention mechanisms. In human society, the actors that historically competed to hold attention power were media outlets. In contemporary “attention” economies, however, traditional media actors—which rely on human editorial curation and operate within established in- stitutional and legal accountability frameworks—are increasingly superseded by al- gorithmically controlled media, typically centered on recommender systems and social media platforms. These digital media platforms modulate information flow in far more opaque and inaccessible ways; although they are not wholly outside legal and regulatory frameworks, their forms of accountability remain partial, contested, and unevenly enforceable. A further extension to our account involves focusing on the actors who maintain registering power. With the advent of regulatory technology (RegTech), distributed ledgers and smart contract infrastructures have increasingly entered the institutional operational cycle.
