For systemic maintenance, we expect the existence of some enforcement mechanism (generally coupled with reinforcement) that is able to guide and maintain, to a large extent, individuals who are in principle independent to form an assemblage. Consider again the symbiosis example: the contextual obligation of interaction is a consequence of the positive reward of such an organization with respect to the absence of interaction. Enforcement actions generalize this principle by either circumscribing undesir- able behaviour through the prevention of its possibility (ex-ante enforcement) or providing an institutional response to failures that strengthens general compliance through rewards and sanctions (ex-post enforcement). Traditionally, ex-ante en- forcement serves as a core mechanism for authorization systems, whereas ex-post enforcement appears more prominently in judicial systems. However, enforcement is not necessarily driven solely by legal mechanisms, but also by social or physical dispositions (e.g., regulations regarding right-hand or left- hand traffic are backed by a form of “natural” enforcement: not complying with the correct driving direction carries direct and potentially severe consequences). Yet, legal transactions have the advantage of foregrounding explicit protections against the risks of a lack of coordination between the parties. The general evolution of contemporary enforcement practices—observable not only in modern legal systems, but also in schools, parenting, and informal groupings— has been nicely synthesized by Dari-Mattiacci and Geest (2013) as “the rise of car- rots and the decline of sticks”. The authors propose a theory of this process, showing that, from an economic perspective, punishment-based systems are more efficient in simple settings, i.e., when (i) the burden of compliance can be well specified (or, in other words, it is simple to verify whether a certain behavior is compliant with the rules) and (ii) is fairly distributed among the involved parties. Reward-based systems, on the other hand, are more efficient when the regulator has difficulties specifying the burden, or if the burden is highly skewed against a few social partici- pants (becoming, in practice, a negative lottery). As modern societies become more complex, the heterogeneity of contexts and tasks is increasing, making reward-based systems increasingly prevalent. But why does this happen? At first glance, we could write any contract either carrot-style or stick-style and they would be identical, at least from an algebraic point of view. However, experiments conducted in behavioral economics on fram- ing have demonstrated that formally similar gains and losses are not experienced or evaluated symmetrically (Kahneman and Tversky, 1979). Even at the analyti- cal level, Dari-Mattiacci and De Geest observe that there is an intrinsic difference Anchoring Distributed Agency: Institutional Metaphors and AI Techniques 25 due to the monitoring component: if monitoring is not perfect, the two formula- tions are different because a party that is not monitored in a carrot-based system counts as non-compliant; whereas, in a stick-based system, it counts as compliant. In practice, as observed by Boer (2014), a reward regime assumes that most peo- ple are non-compliant; while a punishment regime assumes that most people are compliant. Boer then proposes the following evidence criteria to decide whether an enforcement system is based on carrots or on sticks: • a reward regime requires the production of evidence of compliance; • a punishment regime requires the production of evidence of non-compliance. These criteria shift the attention from internal, subjective aspects relative to the par- ties to external aspects specified in regulations. Interestingly, these mechanisms are related to the burden of proof (see section 3.3), usually distributed among claimants (for evidence of non-compliance) and addressees (for evidence of compliance). 5 Pluralism as Ecological Diversity 5.1 Epistemological Pluralism Interestingly, the dichotomy totality versus assemblage also helps with understand- ing the distinction between formal and informal conceptual systems. The difficulty of constraining natural language in formal semantics is well known. The regularity of association of linguistic terms with a certain interpretation is a consequence of the relative regularity of the environment, of the sensory-motor capabilities, of the knowledge, and of the commitments of the communicating actors—but a change in one of those aspects might entail a change in those associations as well. Taking this phenomenon into account means accepting epistemological pluralism. Furthermore, beyond inter-agent pluralism (agents, being independent, share nei- ther the same knowledge nor the same interests or evaluative frameworks), there is also an intra-agent pluralism to be considered, stemming from ontological stratifi- cation (Boer, 2009). For instance, a road may be seen as a curved line while looking at directions on a map, as a surface while driving, or as a volume when laying asphalt to construct it. These alternative conceptual cuts, reminiscent of Dennett’s stances, depend on which properties of the entity are relevant to the task at hand. Successful alignment of vocabularies or ontologies requires an adequate analysis of the underlying commitments associated with the task domain. Normative systems, which are symbolically defined, inherently suffer from this problem, as the possible contexts in which they might operate cannot be fully an- ticipated. Yet at the same time, they provide a prototypical solution to the issue, by attempting to consolidate goals into a higher-order, abstract form, leaving further contextualization to be specified on demand. 26 Alexander Boer and Giovanni Sileno 5.2 Normative Pluralism But there is another level of assemblage to be taken into account for normativity: agents belong to a single normative system only in an ideal case. Think of all the rules and norms, written and unwritten, that we encounter in daily life. At home we perform certain chores because we at some point agreed to a distribution of them, or perhaps simply because they are expected of us. We followed both traffic rules and informal driving etiquette on the roads while traveling to and from work. We parked the car following rules and directions, greeted colleagues following social conventions, and perhaps followed directions about where not to smoke, where not to drink our coffee, and where to discard our paper coffee cup. Finally, we are writ- ing this chapter following grammar and spelling rules, instructions about structuring chapters, and conventions about citation and plagiarism, all while working to meet a deadline. These norms belong to different types, and we recognize them as part of various complex normative systems. Some are based in law, others in the social conventions of society at large, in the conventions of the academic field, those of a particular building, or even of a small private circle. Any of these norms we may have noticed or overlooked, regarded or disregarded, and followed or violated, con- sciously or unconsciously. And for the most part we hardly think about them—a circumstance which, when we do pause to consider it, is truly remarkable. Normative pluralism poses two central questions (see, e.g., Twining, 2010). The first question is: how do we notice norms, and detect and resolve conflicts between pairs of norms as they arise? When two norms are in conflict, they do so because they either: • disaffirm each other, i.e., appear to label the same intention as both strongly per- mitted and impermissible, or • require us to adopt two intentions that are jointly inconsistent with our beliefs and thus cannot be executed simultaneously if our beliefs are correct—for example, requiring that we both keep our cake untouched and that we eat it. Norms can be grouped into a normative order—an institutionalized system of norms aimed at ordering social relationships among members of a community or group. Conflicts between these norms are generally ironed out within the system itself, with meta-rules for determining the applicability and priority of norms. This is, however, only possible to the extent that agreed-upon norms for conflict resolu- tion and prioritization can be established within the community or group, provided that recognizing norm applicability is not itself the overriding concern, and that the outcomes of the conflict resolution process remain acceptable to the members of the community (i.e., the right norms are applied). Anchoring Distributed Agency: Institutional Metaphors and AI Techniques 27 5.3 Value Pluralism The second question posed by normative pluralism is: how do we measure how norms perform overall if they are to be effective in a plurality of norm environments? Systems of norms range from public ones, with universal appeal, to the most private. Thus, the problem of measuring norm performance is relevant at all levels of gran- ularity, and from both intra-agent and inter-agent perspectives. Individual agents, organizations, and whole communities form judgments about the performance of individual norms, and the problem of forming opinions about individual norms in a plurality of norm environments is rather ill-defined if it is the norm environment itself that frames what rational action is. One might naively view this problem as purely quantitative—namely, as a mat- ter of measuring overall levels of compliance. From the perspective of the values served by norms, however, this is typically ill-advised. A norm performs well if it functions—or is complied with—in the environments where it is useful, and fails or is violated in those environments where its value is outweighed by more important values served by competing norms that should take precedence. As such, aggregate compliance levels are meaningless unless properly scoped to the specific ecological niche in which the norm ought to apply. Modern struggles in AI alignment illustrate this well. The EU AI Act states that “AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way that they achieve an appropriate level of accuracy” (Art 15(1) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689). This re- quirement rarely translates to a simple aggregate accuracy measure. The way of measuring, the scope of the measurements, and the threshold to clear are deter- mined by niche, and some types of error (think of false positives vs. false negatives in simple yes/no decisions) clearly weigh far more heavily than others. Blanket enforcement of guardrails (against racism, uses for adult content cre- ation, bomb-making, or hacking, etc.) on foundational models like LLMs without regard to uses in different niches is problematic. HuggingFace for instance recently made the news when it stated that it had to install a Chinese model (GLM) to be able to evade hacking guardrails in order to defend against being hacked by an OpenAI AI system12. The guardrails do not really contribute to compliance with the accu- racy requirement, which applies to ‘AI systems’ instead of models. Furthermore, multi-agent architectures typically increase the problem. If a model is directly in- terfaced to an end user a 90% accuracy rate for a guardrail may seem superficially acceptable. But serially connect a speech-to-text, LLM, and text-to-speech model and the guardrails of the models may already falsely trip (assuming independence) up to approximately 30% (1−0.93) of the time, and become a practical obstacle to third party development of agentic AI using commercially available models. 12 https://huggingface.co/blog/security-incident-july-2026 28 Alexander Boer and Giovanni Sileno 5.4 Pluralisms and Ecological Diversity A general pattern can be traced at this point. Intra-agent epistemological plural- ism emerges from simplifying the agent-environment coupling relative to functional niches, thereby driving the explicit articulation of multiple agent-environment cou- plings; in other words, a single agent may require different conceptualisations of the same environment for different tasks and roles. Inter-agent pluralism aggregates these articulations—and the commitments exploiting them—resulting in a set of agent-roles available within a social niche. Normative and value pluralism can be seen as components of the former, aggregating social coordination (institutional) and reward model aspects, respectively. Related forms include political pluralism, which is widely regarded as an important condition of democratic life, and legal plu- ralism, which becomes especially salient where multiple legal orders, jurisdictions, or normative authorities overlap (e.g. jurisdiction in international matters). All these forms of pluralism arise naturally when adopting an ecological view of social systems: they mirror the diversity of aspects across social niches available within a society at a given point in time. This implies that rules can be understood and modelled only within the context of social roles (which are, in turn, associ- ated with specific niches). Any effort to capture regularities, rules, or associated epiphenomena without considering the niche using them is bound to fail, because as soon as the relative distribution of niches in society changes, the foundations of the model will change as well. This observation is compatible with accounts emphasiz- ing the material dimension of law, according to which law is primarily constituted and performed out of dedicated practices pertaining to a certain social assemblage (Gordon, Rieder, and Sileno, 2022; Philippopoulos-Mihalopoulos, 2014; Pottage, 2012). Conversely, from a system-design perspective, this view entails that all ar- tifacts capturing norms (norm as in normativity, but also as in normality) need to be considered in an ecologically sound computational architecture, able to assimi- late or accommodate adequately any environmental configuration, that is, capable of representing and handling concerns of norm applicability, interpretation, and re- vision. This requirement suggests introducing an explicit normware design level for artificial devices, extending the distinction between hardware and software (Sileno, 2026; Sileno, Boer, and van Engers, 2018).

sections.heading: 6 Discussion
sections.text: 6.1 Institutional Metaphors for Large-Scale Distributed AI With the increasing use of distributed, computational, and possibly autonomous systems—such as those employed in Agentic AI—as well as technologies based on distributed ledgers/smart contracts, the Internet of Things, and digital twins, it is relevant to apply the preceding conceptualizations to assess the extent to which the Anchoring Distributed Agency: Institutional Metaphors and AI Techniques 29 institutional mechanisms identified in the legal domain find correspondence within computational social systems. Agentic AI As observed throughout this chapter, the rapid deployment of Agentic AI presents an operational testbed for institutional metaphors. In these systems, LLMs are wrapped within a software harness or scaffolding managing execution loops, mem- ory buffers, external tool calls, and guardrail enforcement. System prompts and guardrail policies may function as norms (N) when they guide or constrain con- duct; shared records, authorised workflow states, or ledger entries may function as institutional facts (F) when they are treated as authoritative within the relevant ar- rangement. An agent harness, although generally specified in terms of workflow, functions rather as an electronic institution, as it can be used to define operational boundaries, interaction protocols, and power distributions across heterogeneous ac- tors. Contemporary architectures, however, frequently suffer from structural flaws derived from primitive organizational systems. First, many default workflows have used the same underlying LLM both to gener- ate a solution and to verify it. As noted in Section 3.2, effective verification depends on forms of independence, such as information asymmetry and distinct evaluative biases. When generator and verifier share identical parametric knowledge and con- text buffers, verification collapses into sycophancy or defensive rationalizations due to confirmation bias rather than critical oversight. Contemporary architectures in- creasingly address this failure mode by integrating heterogeneous pipelines includ- ing non-generative models—such as Jev-like discriminative models, JEPA-based world models, or formal theorem provers (Lean, Coq, etc.). Second, computer science traditionally focuses on ex-ante enforcement mechanisms— hardcoding constraints through, for instance, schema validation, API tool-masking, or interceptors that inhibit agent affordances (A) prior to execution. This approach conflates deontic prohibitions (what an agent ought not to do) with potestative dis- abilities (what an agent cannot do). As multi-agent systems scale in complexity, however, verifying every step via assertion may become not only computationally prohibitive, but also operationally brittle, or overly restrictive, as it may disable valid agent affordances under edge cases (see the discussion in the operating sys- tems paragraph). Techniques like Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) have been introduced to accommodate contexts where rules cannot be easily hardcoded; yet, bottom-up mechanisms for preference aggregation fail to match the top-down authoritative mechanisms observable in legal systems. In this context, designing agent harnesses with the right combination of procedural mechanisms and case- centred contextualization points—such as explicit escalation roles and institutional appeal protocols—would allow higher-order processes and human overseers to eval- uate reasons for failure and dynamically reallocate burdens of proof, echoing human legal systems. 30 Alexander Boer and Giovanni Sileno Smart contracts Despite their name, “smart contracts” (see, e.g., De Filippi, Wray, and Sileno, 2020) neither embody any problem-solving methodology nor are specified by assigning normative positions to parties as in conventional contracts. Their primary innova- tion, much like the blockchain, is the distributed ledger, which is utilized for both “contract” publication and the registration of related transactions, thereby remov- ing the requirement for an explicit third-party maintainer (e.g., a bank, public ad- ministration, or notary). Consequently, they lay the groundwork for a potential in- frastructural centralization of registration power. However, by collapsing normative functions into the implementation layer, these artifacts remain in practice unintelli- gible to users. Furthermore, they fail to provide by design architectural mechanisms allowing interpretative power to exercise negative feedback on directive power in novel or exceptional contexts not anticipated at design time. This limitation severely undermines their suitability for institutional operationalization. Operating systems (at large) In recent years, many efforts have been directed toward the development of se- cure operating systems. Traditionally, most implementations build upon solutions in the spirit of access control lists (ACLs)—mapping each user and object to the set of operations they are permitted to perform (e.g., read, write, execute) (Fer- raiolo, Barkley, and Kuhn, 1999). These permissions are also commonly referred to as privileges or authorizations; however, upon closer inspection, this represents a conflation of the homonymous Hohfeldian positions. Without such permission, a user is disabled from performing the action rather than prohibited.13. By virtue of their dematerialized content, computational systems are not fundamentally differ- ent from institutional systems: both rely on symbol-processing mechanisms. In this sense, writing a file is not merely a physical operation but an institutional one; con- sequently, performing it requires the corresponding institutional power. Capability- based security models implicitly rely on this principle, utilizing communicable to- kens for authorization known as capabilities; see, e.g. (Levy, 1984). The principle of least privilege (or least authorization) requires that capabilities be assigned strictly according to the actual operational requirements of the application. However, treating authorization solely as power introduces further complexities. In socio-legal settings, permission is most commonly invoked when an agent pos- sesses the (typically physical) power to perform an action A but is legally prohibited from doing so (e.g. you are permitted to smoke when it is generally prohibited to). More generally, permissions are introduced because power lacks the necessary gran- ularity to capture outcomes and higher-order systemic effects, whereas prohibition can capture those. For instance, while a single action per se may be permitted (en- abled), that action within a sequence or in combination with others may yield unau- 13 For a formal analysis of the interaction between deontic and potestative categories, see e.g. Sileno, Pascucci, and Markovich (2023). Anchoring Distributed Agency: Institutional Metaphors and AI Techniques 31 thorized results (consider, for example, denial-of-service (DoS) attacks exploiting trusted applications).14 Failure cases extracted from ex-post evaluations can be used effectively to mon- itor preparations for known failure schemes. However, the fundamental problem— addressed in human societies through deontic directives—is establishing principled reasons as an institutional anchor to qualify new types of failure (or to create new qualification rules) within an existing normative framework. Organizations heav- ily struggle to maintain alignment across their official AI policies, instructions for use (IFU) for human operators, system prompts governing LLMs, instructions for monitoring agents, and hard access controls. As a result, they remain ill-prepared to integrate lessons learned in a timely manner or adapt their governance frame- works when unexpected edge cases arise. Clearly separating deontic and potestative dimensions is a first step necessary to overcome these difficulties. Reinforcement learning, and genetic algorithms In the last decade, major results have been obtained through the hybrid application of deep learning methods and reinforcement learning (starting from AlphaGo (Silver et al., 2016)). Genetic algorithms address related optimisation problems, through evolutionary selection over candidate solutions. Most of these approaches depend on centralized evaluative mechanisms—reward functions, fitness functions, or pref- erence models—that determine which outcomes count as better or worse. These types of feedback represent only two among the six primitive reward and punish- ment regimes identifiable in institutional systems (see Sileno, 2016, sec. 9.5), but, independently of their type, the deeper obstacle to generalising such mechanisms is the difficulty of specifying a general feedback function. AI researchers and practitioners (and problem-solvers more generally) tend to as- sume that identifying goals is the easy part, whereas determining how to reach those targets is the hard part. However, when conceiving applications required to adapt to users or social environments, this presumption rapidly collapses—and necessarily so—for at least three key reasons: (a) the multiplicity of preference configurations among social participants, (b) the highly contextual nature of these configurations, and (c) the predominantly tacit character of human preferences. To some extent, RLHF belongs to this same architectural lineage, although it aggregates feedback from diverse human annotators. This raises a fundamental un- derlying question: what is the specific operational niche to which this feedback is anchored? While majority voting or reward-model averaging can successfully iso- late recurrent patterns across annotators, this aggregation mechanism risks collaps- 14 As an additional example of engineering “blindness” to social semantics, consider the endless discussions regarding which logical fragment should be adopted for knowledge representation on the Semantic Web—focusing primarily on computability and the halting problem—disregarding the fact that as soon as an external interface is opened via SPARQL, the system can be rendered inoperable by a DoS attack, regardless of the logical fragment employed. 32 Alexander Boer and Giovanni Sileno ing the niche-alignment problem into alignment with merely the most statistically represented niche. General critique and the role of AI & Law A recurrent limitation of contemporary AI lies in trying to capitalize too much on optimizing and reasoning about evidential input and options for action (generate & test paradigm, or in more recent terminology, generate & verify) within known requirements, constraints, and problem formulations, rather than examining the un- derlying phenomena of niche construction, adaptiveness, and the derivation of re- quirements linked to social roles. Deciding to target social roles rather than for- mulating requirements on an individual basis follows from Heiner’s theory and is cognitively supported by the observation that humans actually perform better at de- ontic reasoning than at evidential reasoning (Mercier and Sperber, 2011), acquiring this capability earlier in childhood. Interestingly, the AI & Law discipline (Bench-Capon et al., 2012) can be thought of as originating from reversing this general AI attitude—that is, by focusing strongly on conflicts between goals and the mechanisms by which we acquire and select them (normativity). Capitalizing on this experience, even if considering the automatic discovery of ecological niches too ambitious, one could still aim for the automated design of compositions of social roles intended to achieve specific given requirements. The core problem in constructing such systems lies in detecting and resolving internal role conflicts by internalizing epistemological, normative, and value pluralism as a design issue rather than just a monitoring one. A critical de- sign challenge involves establishing adequate data and knowledge roles—those that mediate data and knowledge flows between behavioral niches. An improvident cen- tralization of data, for instance, might enable the utilization of collected informa- tion for purposes unintended by the data-providing agents. This reveals the need for a principle of data-information minimization, whereby the provision and collec- tion of data are calibrated against the adequacy of reasons for accessing information (conditioned upon the social role attributed to the requestor and its accompanying social context), rather than relying on a token-based principle of least privilege tied solely to the requestor. In other words, this calls for a fundamental reconsideration of the attribution of responsibility to computational entities and social stakeholders (see, e.g., Sileno et al., 2020). 6.2 AI Techniques for Running Institutions 6.2.1 Confronting inadequate simplifications in a complex world With globalization, all socio-economic actors (private individuals, private compa- nies, NGOs, and public institutions) became increasingly active at an international Anchoring Distributed Agency: Institutional Metaphors and AI Techniques 33 scale, and institutional interdependencies have transitioned from exceptional to stan- dard operating conditions. Operating concurrently within multiple legal jurisdic- tions, these actors are subject to an ever-changing web of rules (e.g., national provi- sions, international treaties, standards), whose complexity naturally increases with the volume of international activities undertaken. This carries risks of normative misalignment, which may expose such actors to enforcement penalties and institu- tions to systemic failures. On the other hand, as their activities occur at an interna- tional level, those actors can establish practices—for instance, aiming to reduce the burden of compliance with environmental, labour, or privacy regulations, or imple- menting schemes of tax avoidance, tax evasion, or money laundering—that are not yet recognized by—or remain opaque to— formal institutions at the national level. Far from simplifying the operational environment, contemporary geopolitical disruptions are just increasing systemic complexity. Because of the deep transna- tional interdependence, political, socio-economic, and environmental shocks remain no longer isolated; and socio-economic actors find themselves in an increasingly turbulent environment. From a theoretical perspective, an increase in complexity means an increase in the C-D gap for agents, and therefore creates pressure toward the establishment of simpler, more manageable operational rules—at the potential expense of the nor- mative elaboration conducted upfront and of the diversity of cases that may occur, cases that would otherwise require a dedicated response to properly serve the in- terests of citizens. In this context, AI, and in particular AI & Law, could provide methodological and computational support for consolidating the rational function- ing of collective agencies. Beyond classic problem-solving tasks for operational purposes (e.g., planning, scheduling), here we refer in particular to methods supporting higher-order func- tions of rational agency as those highlighted above. For instance, in current prac- tices, one can observe little attention to pluralism within organizational settings, driven by an exclusive focus on the implementation and optimization of “normal” provision patterns—the so-called happy flow. Consequently, even though the pre- sumption of compliance utilized at the rule design phase is generally untested, pat- terns of failure are relegated outside the scope of attention. Thus, even if numerically negligible, failures in service delivery consume an increasingly disproportionate share of resources, thereby generating the well-documented phenomena associated with machine bureaucracy (see, for instance, Seddon, 2008). Symptomatic of this situation are unrealistic methods for quantifying and mea- suring performance, a general disregard for the systemic significance of failures, and the absence of systematic diagnostic processes capable of mitigating operational burdens (see, e.g. Sileno, Boer, and van Engers, 2017). Alongside this, excessive expectations regarding the insights derivable from big data analytics remain funda- mentally implausible, precisely because the specific social niches in which data is generated are completely neglected. On the opposite side, collective agencies may risk adopting an attitude of para- lyzing realism when they pay excessive attention to capturing societal pluralism at an overly fine granularity, rendering them incapable of completing the requirements 34 Alexander Boer and Giovanni Sileno aggregation phase necessary to advance to the directive, operational, or regulative stages. Both the machine-bureaucracy and paralyzing-realism scenarios stem from fail- ing to establish an adequate systematization of environmental modeling—whether through under-modeling or over-modeling. The solution lies in building appropri- ate networks to distribute the burden of capturing social requirements and non- compliance scenarios, ensuring these insights are transmitted, maintained, and pro- cessed to support both the design and development phases and ongoing opera- tional execution (e.g., through automated model-based interpretation and diagnos- tics (Boer and van Engers, 2011a,b; Sileno, 2016; Sileno, Boer, and van Engers, 2017)). These vulnerabilities are complementarily increased by the rapid entrenchment of contemporary AI tools—particularly Generative AI—into public administration and organizational operations at large (see e.g. (Engstrom et al., 2020)). Organiza- tions increasingly rely on proprietary, LLM-driven systems to synthesize evidence, draft policy options, evaluate claims, and interface with the public. This tendency shifts organizational agency toward external computational intermediaries, intro- ducing significant structural dependencies. On a geopolitical scale, this exposes or- ganizations to technological lock-in, extraterritorial regulatory shifts, and vulnera- bilities in operational continuity. At cognitive and societal levels, uncritical adoption risks eroding institutional memory, flattening local context, and inducing systemic confirmation bias among human decision-makers (Cobbe, Lee, and Singh, 2021). When administrative staff accept automated recommendations as baseline truths—a phenomenon driven by cognitive offloading under high workloads—the deliberative capacity of the institution diminishes (Alon-Barkat and Busuioc, 2023; Goddard, Roudsari, and Wyatt, 2012). Rather than enhancing administrative rationality, the uncritical integration of AI models risks entrenching existing biases and institution- alizing forms of bureaucratic alienation. 6.2.2 Possible lines of action AI research, particularly within AI & Law and related tracks, offers a constructive path forward by operationalizing these mechanisms into a computational architec- ture. First, exploiting case law and judicial precedents (or functionally similar do- mains, i.e. use/failure cases and precedent organizational decisions), computational frameworks for narrative and argumentation analysis can help organizations to identify respectively relevant sequences of events and reasons (e.g. factors for de- cisions). These can be further studied to track jurisdictional drift, and model the evolution of the normative systems, and will enable organizations to move beyond brittle ex-ante rule codification, establishing principled reasons to qualify new fail- ure modes as they arise in real-world practice. Second, AI & Law provides in principle conceptual tools to replace rigid, lin- ear workflows with adaptive organizational architectures. For instance, by embed- Anchoring Distributed Agency: Institutional Metaphors and AI Techniques 35 ding operational mechanisms such as recourse, appeal, and overruling directly into multi-agent harnesses, computational systems may automatically trigger a post-hoc audit when a failure is detected, dynamically reallocating burdens of proof, to or- chestrate the interpretation of that failure and possibly revisions of policy. In other words, rather than treating failures as external anomalies, incorporating these feed- back mechanisms help organizations to integrate lessons learned across policy lay- ers, system prompts, access controls, and so on. Third, by leveraging appropriate computational representations, AI & Law en- ables the construction of context-aware executable specifications of norms. Con- temporary language technologies may reduce, though not eliminate, the traditional knowledge-acquisition bottleneck. The resulting normative models allow statutory provisions, which are inherently open-textured in natural language, to be interpreted and operationalized within the specific operational niches where agents interact. When deployed as the governing infrastructure for NMAS, these frameworks reg- ulate commitments (C), affordances (A), expectations (E), and susceptibilities (S), providing accountability by design and thus without reducing governance either to rigid ex-ante constraints or to unmonitored adaptation. Simulation provides a further opportunity. Organisations may use models to stress-test candidate contracts, poli- cies, or organisational procedures against environmental shocks; evaluate risk pro- files ex ante; and identify where execution requires additional safeguards or dispute- resolution mechanisms. 6.3 Converging Opportunities A central challenge in operationalizing AI within institutional contexts lies in estab- lishing intelligible intervention points that guarantee meaningful human oversight without degrading efficiency and effectiveness. From a dual perspective, however, we can say that proper and robust institutional design requires preserving and strate- gically engineering “constructive frictions”: points at which decisions can be ques- tioned, evidence inspected, reasons articulated, and authority reallocated. Despite the enthusiasm for large-scale data-driven analytics, as well as the seem- ingly general-purposiveness of LLM-centered tools, the qualitative depth of knowl- edge available to and applicable-by decision-makers within collective agencies can- not substantially improve on its own. Qualitative depth can be captured only through more principled modeling and simulation methods targeting social niches, com- bined with knowledge maintenance, refinement, reconciliation, and alignment tech- niques. This approach directly reduces our C-D gap, thereby providing robust sup- port for designing more intelligent organizational rules, that is, rules backed by ex- plicit reasons and better situated with respect to their operational environments. Privacy provides an exemplary, instructive testbed for these considerations, as it requires modeling norms governing information use within niches and flows be- tween niches (cf. contextual integrity, Nissenbaum, 2009). More importantly, how- ever, in the last few years calls have emerged for AI governance and AI assurance, 36 Alexander Boer and Giovanni Sileno to ensure that not only privacy, but also fairness, explainability, and contestabil- ity interests of stakeholders are adequately protected in automated decision-making systems utilizing machine learning techniques. These requirements depend heavily on the material conditions of the specific social niche. Skin color, for instance, is functionally relevant when purchasing cosmetics, and gender matters in dating ap- plications, whereas both characteristics are highly problematic in hiring decisions. While it is sometimes assumed that fairness and explainability can be implemented via technical AI methods, in operational practice these requirements are rarely im- plemented with AI techniques at all. They are typically discovered through iterative risk assessment and defined by the burdens of proof dictated by the scenario. From this practical perspective, fairness can be reframed as a property of the input data–its representativeness (of population, of outcomes, of utility, ...), labeling, and selection. Explainability maps instead to a narrative obligation; first justifying why statistics- based decision-making is acceptable in this context at all, and then justifying why the specific decision is defensible. Technical fixes, moreover, tend to displace the compliance problem onto the technique itself rather than resolve it, and their appro- priateness must in any case be weighed against e.g. privacy considerations, as they may inadvertently expose sensitive information (see e.g. Chang and Shokri, 2020). Addressing privacy and AI governance requires modeling underlying norms, in- stitutionalizing attention to system failures, and adopting a diagnostic perspective toward organizations and their institutional goals. This posture is increasingly re- flected in risk-tiered regulatory frameworks such as the EU AI Act, which make documentation, human oversight, and iterative risk management central to compli- ance. In light of the preceding conceptualizations, a natural starting point for this inno- vation is a sufficiently rich methodology for describing and reasoning about social roles, such as those captured by CAES and Hohfeldian positions (DCPL). Because normative positions can shape commitments, affordances, expectations, and susceptibilities, CAES/DCPL descriptions provide a framework for understand- ing role players as boundedly rational agents. Consequently, they can be used to characterize the operational problems—such as modeling, design, planning, moni- toring, diagnosis, and assessment (see, e.g. Breuker, 1994)— that agents must solve within a given social role, along with the knowledge resources required to do so. The greater the problem complexity (viewed through the lens of the C-D gap), the more difficult it becomes for an observer to verify whether an agent is acting as expected. To address this, the agent must articulate and defend its choices to other participants in the environment to demonstrate correct conduct. Evidently, an agent in a given role is inherently biased in its information gathering by its CAES descrip- tion requirements. Therefore, correctly assessing ex-post whether the agent reached sound decisions often requires evaluating rationality at a higher level through the dialectical interplay between agents. A standard solution, compatible with Heiner’s theory of predictable behavior, involves establishing increasingly rigorous burden of proof protocols for justifying decisions. Conversely, when performance can be read- ily scored (such as in facial recognition tasks), the requisite depth of the articulated reasoning process remains minimal. This brings us to a fundamental design choice: Anchoring Distributed Agency: Institutional Metaphors and AI Techniques 37 deciding whether to employ tacit knowledge methods (typically statistical and feed- forward) or explicit knowledge methods. Naturally, the former are inherently faster than the latter; however, speed is not the only value at stake. For Watson-like systems, the results of the question-answering “race” among competing agents are straightforward: the human arbiter or judge is presumed to know the answer, and there are typically no demands to explain why that answer is correct. Along similar lines, consider a facial recognition application for unlocking a smartphone. By contrast, when a diagnostic system concludes that “the patient has appendicitis,” it is natural for the user to demand why, expecting reasons that are in- telligible and acceptable within that domain. Similarly, a public administration can- not (or at least ought not to) deny a parking permit or citizenship application without supplying explicit justification. The social role required of intelligent agents across these two classes of applications is fundamentally distinct, and this divergence lies at the root of contemporary calls for explainable AI (Miller, 2019). When AI sys- tems assume socially consequential roles, the relevant question is not whether every internal computation can be exposed, but whether the system can provide the kinds of reasons, evidence, and review mechanisms that its institutional role requires. To conclude, if we solve the social-role acquisition problem, we can solve the explainable AI problem (at least in its societal dimension), because we will be able to identify a higher-order burden of proof (and associated protocols) that can be used to distribute computation to specialized agents. This problem lies at the core of our difficulties in designing complex, adaptive AI systems, as illustrated by the con- fused use of knowledge structures throughout the history of AI. Moreover, solving the social-role acquisition problem will also improve the functioning of our insti- tutions, providing a better environmental model with which to implement and test new institutional mechanisms, and through which to interpret social data. Automating the social role acquisition problem from scratch would require the acquiring agent to be embedded in the social system in the same—or a very similar—way as humans are. This is currently not a realizable condition, for major technical and social obstacles. However, a first step toward solving the social-role acquisition problem is realizable: considering as primary design source the collec- tive requirements as those that communities reify in institutions, and applying the lessons learned therefrom in engineering.
